class: center, middle
#Research question: 
## To what extent has the length of stay in mental health hospitals in Scotland changed over the past 2 decades?

---

class: inverse, center, middle
# About our dataset

---

# Mental health inpatient activity

- Data from "Public Health Scotland"

- Consists of 14 files containing information on patients with mental health problems

- All patients had been cared for as inpatient or day cases in Scottish general and psychiatric hospitals for all NHS Boards or residence and treatment

- Period covered is financial years 1997/98 - 2021/22

- We chose this dataset because there were many variables that could be linked together so we could come up with many different questions and relationships to analyse

---

#Initial steps

- Form possible relationships between different variables and brainstorm research questions that we could explore further

- Create summary statistics and data visualisations from our initial ideas to see if there are any trends or if it would be worth investigating further

- Look for ways to link the datasets to obtain our chosen variables

---

#Brainstorming ideas

- Factors we could look at:

 - Age, sex, diagnosis, frequency of stay, number of admissions, patient count, discharge count
 
- Initial questions:
  
  - Has treatment for mental health changed?
  
  - Has the ratio of male and females changed?
  
  - Has awareness of mental health changed?
  
  - How has the length of stay changed?
  
- Could compare factors between different financial years or regions
  
---

#Biases and how we avoided them

- Initial biases we confronted was we assumed there would be relationships between specific variables and we predicted trends for these relationships

 - Assumed number of patients would increase in hospitals due to increasing population
 
  - Ended up being incorrect after calculating summary statistics
 
 - Assumed length of stay would decrease due to "improved treatment methods" that arises from experience and more research over the years

- How we proceeded our investigation

 - We decided to use data from every hospital in Scotland instead of specific regions
 
  - Helped reduce selection bias and accurately represent the diversity of cases and treatment approaches across the entire healthcare system

 - Made sure to only explore trends we found from summary statistics or data visualisations instead of our own assumptions to ensure our answer is not influenced by bias

---

#Cleaning and processing our data

- Renamed frequently used datasets to be more effective at showing the variables and information contained

- Filtered each dataset to contain the area code for Scotland 

 - Found an area code that consisted of all the hospitals in Scotland instead of individual regions

- Filtered each dataset to group different variables together

 - Eg. financial year, age, length of stay

- Renamed diagnosis variables from codes to the diagnosis names

 - Made it more clear when plotting graphs
 
---
#Processing diagnosis data

```{r}
diagnosis <- diagnosis %>% mutate(
              DiagnosisName = case_when(
                ICD10Codes == "F00 - F09 or Chapter G and second position F00" ~ "Organic, including symptomatic, mental disorders",
                ICD10Codes == "F10 - F19" ~ "Mental & behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use",
                ICD10Codes == "F20 - F29" ~ "Schizophrenia, schizotypal, & delusional disorders",
                ICD10Codes == "F30 - F39" ~ "Mood (affective) disorders",
                ICD10Codes == "F40 - F49" ~ "Neurotic, stress-related, & somatoform disorders",
                ICD10Codes == "F60 - F69" ~ "Disorders of adult personality & behaviour",
                ICD10Codes == "F50 - F59, F70 - F99" ~ "Other selected diagnoses principally affecting children & young people"
               )
              )
```


.footnotes[
To respect the data and the people, we added a column to the dataset with the diagnosis name that was relating to each of the diagnosis codes. This makes it easier to understand what the graph is showing, without having to memorise what each of the codes stand for. 
]

---

class: inverse, center, middle

# Our data visualisations

---
```{r warning=FALSE, fig.height=6, fit.width=12, echo=FALSE}
#Bar chart for number of patients vs. financial year
age.sex %>% 
  filter(HBR == "S92000003") %>%
  group_by(FinancialYear, Sex) %>%
  summarise(amount = sum(PatientsCount),.groups="drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = FinancialYear, 
             x = amount, 
             fill = Sex)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Financial Year",
       y = "Number of Patients",
       title = "Number of Patients vs Financial Year")+theme_minimal()
```
.footnotes[
- This is a graph showing the total number of patients in each year from our dataset. The proportion of male to females roughly remains the same throughout the years. 
]


---

```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=FALSE}
age.sex %>% filter(HBR == "S92000003",
                       FinancialYear == "1997/98" | 
                       FinancialYear == "2021/22") %>%
                   group_by(FinancialYear, AgeGroup) %>%
                   summarise(Amount = sum(PatientsCount),.groups="drop") %>%
                   mutate(
                     Order = case_when(
                       AgeGroup == "0-17 years" ~ 1,
                       AgeGroup == "18-24 years" ~ 2,
                       AgeGroup == "25-39 years" ~ 3,
                       AgeGroup == "40-64 years" ~ 4,
                       AgeGroup == "65plus years" ~ 5
                     )
                   ) %>%
                   ggplot(aes(x = reorder(AgeGroup, +Order), y = Amount)) +
                   facet_wrap(vars(FinancialYear)) +
                   geom_bar(position = "dodge", stat = "identity",fill="forestgreen") +
                   theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=0.9)) +
                   labs(x = "Age of Patients", 
                        y = "Amount of Patients", 
                        title = "Changes in Age of Patients", 
                        subtitle = "from 1997 to 2022",
                        caption = "From 76290 patients in 1997 to 61030 patients in 2022"
                        )+theme_minimal()
```

.footnotes[
- A significant drop can be seen in the number of patients aged 25-39 years in the year 2021/22 as compared to 1997/98. The number of patients aged 0-17 years and 18-24 years old have also dropped.
]
---

```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12,out.height="90%", echo=FALSE}
length.of.stay %>% filter(HBT == "S92000003",
                       FinancialYear == "1997/98" | 
                       FinancialYear == "2021/22") %>%
                   group_by(FinancialYear, LengthOfStay) %>%
                   summarise(Amount = sum(NumberOfStays),.groups = "drop") %>%
                   mutate(
                     Order = case_when(
                       LengthOfStay == "< 1 day" ~ 1,
                       LengthOfStay == "1 - 7 days" ~ 2,
                       LengthOfStay == "8 - 28 days" ~ 3,
                       LengthOfStay == "29 days - 6 months" ~ 4,
                       LengthOfStay == "> 6 months" ~ 5
                     )
                   ) %>%
                   ggplot(aes(x = reorder(LengthOfStay, +Order), y = Amount)) +
                   facet_wrap(vars(FinancialYear)) +
                   geom_bar(position = "dodge", stat = "identity",fill="forestgreen") +
                   theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=0.9)) +
                   labs(x = "Length of Patients Stay", 
                        y = "Amount of Patients", 
                        title = "Changes in Lengths of Stay", 
                        subtitle = "from 1997 to 2022",
                        caption = "From 76290 patients in 1997 to 61030 patients in 2022"
                        )+theme_minimal()

```
.footnotes[
- The number of patients who stayed in the hospital for 8-28 days and 29 days- 6 months decreased a lot in 2021/22 as compared to 1997/98. 
]

---
```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=FALSE}
readmissions.single <- readmissions %>%
  filter(HBT == "S92000003") %>%

readmissions.single %>%
```

```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=FALSE}
#bar chart for 1997/88 and 2021/22 based on diagnoses and amount of patients
diagnosis %>% filter(HBT == "S92000003",
                     FinancialYear == "1997/98" | 
           FinancialYear == "2021/22") %>%
              group_by(FinancialYear, DiagnosisName) %>%
              summarise(amount = sum(PatientsCount),.groups="drop") %>%
              ggplot(aes(x = amount, y = DiagnosisName, fill = FinancialYear)) +
              theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=0.9)) +
              geom_bar(position = "dodge", stat = "identity") +
              labs(y = "Diagnoses in Patients", 
                        x = "Amount of Patients", 
                        title = "Changes in Diagnoses", 
                        subtitle = "from 1997 to 2022",
                        caption = "From 76290 patients in 1997 to 61030 patients in 2022",
                        legend = "Financial Year"
                        )+theme_minimal()
```
---

```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=FALSE}
length.of.stay.single <- length.of.stay %>% 
                   filter(HBT == "S92000003",) %>%
                   group_by(FinancialYear, LengthOfStay) %>%
                   summarise(Amount = sum(NumberOfStays),.groups = "drop") %>%
                   mutate(
                     Midpoint = case_when(
                         LengthOfStay == "< 1 day" ~ 0.5,
                         LengthOfStay == "1 - 7 days" ~ 4,
                         LengthOfStay == "8 - 28 days" ~ 18,
                         LengthOfStay == "29 days - 6 months" ~ 98.5,
                         LengthOfStay == "> 6 months" ~ 168 
                      ),
                     TotalStays = Midpoint * Amount
                   ) %>%
                   group_by(FinancialYear) %>%
                   summarise(TotalStaysYearly = sum(TotalStays), TotalAmount = sum(Amount)) %>%
                   mutate(
                     AverageStay = TotalStaysYearly / TotalAmount,
                     FinancialYear = as.numeric(substr(FinancialYear, 1, 4))
                   )

length.of.stay.single %>%                   
                   ggplot(aes(y = AverageStay, x = FinancialYear)) +
                   geom_point(color="red") +
                   geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,color="black",
                               formula = y ~ x) +
                   theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=0.9)) +
                   labs(x = "Year", 
                        y = "Average Stay", 
                        title = "Changes in Average Stay", 
                        subtitle = "from 1997 to 2022",
                        caption = "From 76290 patients in 1997 to 61030 patients in 2022"
                        )+theme_minimal()
```
---

class: center, middle
```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=TRUE}
model1 <- linear_reg() %>%
          set_engine("lm") %>%
          fit(AverageStay ~ FinancialYear, data = length.of.stay.single)

tidy(model1)
```

.footnotes[
This gives the equation:
Average Stay = 1017 - 0.517(Year)
]

---
```{r warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.width=12, echo=FALSE}
model1_aug <- augment(model1$fit)
ggplot(model1_aug, mapping = aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(color="red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Predicted Average Stay", y = "Residuals", title = "Graph of the Residuals from the Linear Model of Length of Stay")+theme_minimal()
```

---

class: inverse, center, middle

#Back to our question

---

#Our findings

- The average length of stay has decreased by 9 days over the past 2 decades, which is a decrease of approximately 0.5 days each year.

- The number of patients with long stays (8-28 days, 29 days - 6 months, 6+ months) has significantly decreased
 
- Most patients in the year 2021/22 stayed in the hospitals for only up to week, whereas the most common length of stay in 1997/98 was 8 - 28 days. 

- Number of stays which were less than one day have also increased significantly in 2021/22
 
- The percentage of readmissions within 28 days has shown a gradual increase since 2010 however the percentage of re-admissions within 133 days has shown a significant overall decrease since 2000.
 
- This may indicate that treatments may have gotten better and therefore quicker
 
---

#What are the advantages of the investigation we have performed

- The decrease in the lengths of stay over the 2 years suggests that the mental health care system has gotten better and the treatments are now quicker than they were 2 decades ago. The percentage of re-admissions within 133 days has decreased which implies that the healthcare has gotten better, resulting in fewer relapses after treatments. 

- To get a general idea of trend, we chose to use data from all the hospitals in Scotland. This acted as an advantage because it provided a more comprehensive and representative picture of the entire population. This was important to draw conclusions and get a more comprehensive assessment of trends over time, enabling us to identify patterns.

- Reliability and validity of our data: The dataset we used for out analysis was from the official government website. This means that the data was not systematically skewed or influenced by external factors, increasing validity.

---
#What are the limitations/issues of the investigation we have performed?

- As we went on with the research, we kept making new graphs to further answer our questions and analyse the trends. This also means that some of the initial graphs we made may not have a direct correlation with the final answer. 

- Since we used data from all the hospitals in Scotland, we had a lot of data to work with.

- While using data from all hospitals in Scotland increased generalisability, it may have over-generalised the findings.

- Financial year was the only common variable between all of the datasets.
 
- Length of stay was non-continuous data which made it different to calculate summary statistics and plot graphs of it. 

---

#How we respected the four respects

- **Respect the People:** As this data included some medical codes for the different diagnosis, we thought it was a good idea to write out what each of the codes stood for instead, to make the data understandable by everyone. 

- **Respect the Data:** We used appropriate visualisation styles for the data types and made sure every graph was titled, labelled, colored and very easy to interpret.  

- **Respect the Mathematics:** The scale and range of the axes in all the graphs was apt for the data being plotted 

- **Respect the Computers:** We did not overtax the computer. 

---
